newsitem.title: INDIA: Born-again India coalition moves to appease ally.
newsitem.headline: Born-again India coalition moves to appease ally.

text.p: India's United Front coalition, boosted by the Congress party's promise of support, moved on Tuesday to set the foundations of a new government that would outlast its predecessor's brief 10-month reign.
A senior United Front leader said the centre-left alliance planned to create a formal link with its uneasy ally, Congress, in a bid to smooth relations and coordinate policy.
"Once the government is formed, a coordination committee will be there, perhaps," the coalition leader, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"But a final decision has not been taken."

The centre-left United Front was defeated in a confidence vote last Friday following the withdrawal of vital support from Congress, which wanted the 15-party alliance to change its leader as a condition for resuming support.

The front rejected the demand and lost power. But caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, under pressure from regional partners opposed to snap polls, offered on Sunday to quit as United Front leader.
Congress and the United Front formed their uneasy relationship last year to contain Hindu nationalists who scored major gains in general elections that yielded a hung parliament.
When it withdrew its support, Congress accused Deve Gowda of failing to combat the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
On Monday, Congress dropped its own bid for power and agreed to back the United Front under a new leader.
But Congress leader Pranab Mukherjee could not say how long his party would extend its support. "It will depend on their performance," he said.
The alliance's decision-making Steering Committee was expected to name its new leader on Thursday. The group's lawmakers would formally endorse the choice on Sunday.
The United Front official said the coalition expected Congress' support to be stable as its decision on March 30 to abruptly withdraw support had attracted widespread criticism.
"They (Congress) can't repeat the dose without inviting disaster, whatever the provocation," he said.
Last year, Congress agreed to back the United Front to oust a 12-day-old government led by the BJP, which its opponents accuse of bias against India's minority Moslems.
"The main objective is to contain communal forces and avoid mid-term polls," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said.

The BJP is confident it would emerge strengthened from snap elections to the 542-member Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament, where it controls 193 votes with allies. The Congress has 140 members and the United Front 178.
Congress's decision to help vote out Deve Gowda's government has embittered leftwing parties which are not keen to strike another alliance with Congress or bow to its demand to replace its leader.
Somnath Chatterjee, a leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), was quoted on Monday as saying his party might even quit the alliance.
